html:
Fasil Ghebbi is the walled compound of castles and palaces in Gondar, northern Ethiopia, begun by Emperor Fasilides after he made Gondar his capital in 1636. It was the seat of the Ethiopian emperors for about two centuries.

Fasilides came to power after his father Susenyos had turned Catholic under the influence of Portuguese Jesuits, which set off a civil war. Fasilides restored the Orthodox church and expelled the Jesuits. Before him Ethiopian rulers had moved about with their camps; Gondar gave the empire a fixed capital.

The compound holds Fasilides' castle and the buildings of later emperors: palaces, a library, chancery, banquet hall, lion cages and steam baths, all inside a stone wall. Their style mixes local building with Portuguese, Indian and Arab ideas, and the walls are of stone set in lime mortar.

Gondar declined in the 19th century when the emperors lost power to regional lords, and Tewodros II moved away. The site became a World Heritage Site in 1979.
